complete.problem: Trace vectors from magnitude and direction to adding vectors tail to head, the dot product, and lines and planes.
complete.selfExplanation: Explain how a vector carries magnitude and direction in its column vector, how adding vectors tail to head adds the components one pair at a time, how the dot product measures the shadow of one vector on another, and why sliding a free vector does not change it.

steps.annotation: A vector has size and direction: the arrow moves 2 right and 3 up, its column vector records 2 over 3, and the length of the arrow is its magnitude.
steps.text: Step 1 (s1): A vector has size and direction. Watch the arrow move 2 right and 3 up: its column vector records exactly that, 2 over 3, and the length of the arrow is its magnitude. Tell your partner: what two things must two arrows share to be the same vector?

steps.annotation: Adding vectors: tail to head: place the tail of the second vector at the head of the first, and the sum runs from the very first tail to the very last head.
steps.text: Step 2 (s2): Adding vectors: tail to head. Watch vector b slide until its tail meets the head of a: the sum is the one arrow from the very first tail to the very last head, and component by component the right moves add and the up moves add.

steps.annotation: The dot product measures the shadow: drop a perpendicular from the tip of b onto a, and the projection is measured by a . b = |a||b| cos theta.
steps.text: Step 3 (s3): The dot product measures the shadow. Watch the perpendicular drop from the tip of b onto a: the shadow along a is the projection, and a . b = |a||b| cos theta picks out exactly that much of b. When the shadow shrinks to nothing, the vectors are perpendicular and the dot product is zero.

steps.annotation: Lines and planes from a point and directions: one point plus one direction draws a line, r = a + lambda b; a plane needs two directions and its normal stands perpendicular to the whole surface.
steps.text: Step 4 (s4): Lines and planes from a point and directions. One point plus one direction vector draws a whole line: r = a + lambda b, and lambda sweeps every real number to give every point. A plane needs two directions, and its normal vector stands perpendicular to the whole surface.

steps.annotation: A common mistake: moving a vector changes it: sliding a free vector to a new start point leaves it unchanged - only position vectors are pinned to the origin.
steps.text: Step 5 (s5): Here is the trap, sprung on purpose: watch the arrow slide to a new start point and stay the same vector, because free vectors slide. Now work through the worksheet in pairs, checking each answer against the trap section of your student notes. Last, the exit ticket - on your own, no talking - and remember: if you can say why a slid arrow is unchanged, you have cracked today's lesson.

faded.problem: Find the dot product a . b for a = (2, 3) and b = (4, -1).
faded.selfExplanation: The first step is shown. Say how multiplying matching components and adding gives a . b, then why the answer 5 is a scalar, not a vector.

steps.annotation: The scalar a . b = |a||b| cos theta, computed component by component; it measures how much of b points along a, and it is zero exactly when the vectors are perpendicular.
steps.text: Step 1: the dot product multiplies matching components and adds, so write out a . b = 2 x 4 + 3 x (-1).

steps.annotation: The dot product multiplies matching components and adds: 2 x 4 from the right moves and 3 x (-1) from the up moves. It is a scalar, not a vector.
steps.text: Step 3: check the sign: 3 x (-1) = -3, so the total is 8 - 3 = 5, a scalar, not a vector.

paired.problem: A line has vector equation r = (1, 2, 3) + lambda(1, 0, -1). Write down the position vector of the point on the line when lambda = 2.
